chief_complaint: flank pain and visible blood in urine with family history of dialysis
hpi_details: 42F with autosomal dominant family history of ADPKD presenting with acute left flank pain and macrohematuria after cyst hemorrhage.
ideas: She thinks a sharp kidney stone tore something inside her urinary tract as it tried to pass.
concerns: She is terrified that her kidneys are failing and that she will end up dependent on dialysis just like her mother was, threatening her ability to keep working full-time.
expectations: She hopes to get an urgent imaging scan of her kidneys and effective pain medication so she can get back to work.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) with Cyst Hemorrhage evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) with Cyst Hemorrhage is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management for a symptomatic ADPKD cyst hemorrhage centers on supportive care: bed rest, adequate oral hydration, and non-nephrotoxic analgesia, since most hemorrhagic cysts resolve spontaneously within 2-7 days.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: flank pain and visible blood in urine with family history of dialysis
Key HPI features: 42F with autosomal dominant family history of ADPKD presenting with acute left flank pain and macrohematuria after cyst hemorrhage.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 88, Temp 37.0C (afebrile). Bilateral palpable, irregular, enlarged kidneys on abdominal exam; left costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis: 3+ blood, no significant proteinuria, no pyuria or nitrites. Bloods: Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (eGFR ~55), Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL (mildly reduced from baseline 13.5 g/dL). Renal ultrasound/CT shows innumerable bilateral cysts of varying sizes with a hyperdense, hemorrhagic cyst in the left kidney.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) with Cyst Hemorrhage.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Kidney stone without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with flank pain — suggests infected cyst, a more urgent complication.
management_principles: Conservative management: bed rest, oral hydration, and acetaminophen for pain (avoid NSAIDs, which are nephrotoxic and impair platelet function)
Continue antihypertensive therapy (Lisinopril) once hemodynamically stable; avoid anticoagulants during active bleeding
Monitor serial hemoglobin/hematocrit and vital signs for ongoing bleeding; most hemorrhagic cysts resolve spontaneously within 2-7 days
If bleeding is refractory or hemodynamically significant, arrange renal angiography with selective embolization
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 42F with known ADPKD (autosomal dominant family history, including relatives on dialysis) presents with acute-onset left flank pain and gross hematuria, consistent with cyst hemorrhage.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 88, Temp 37.0C (afebrile). Bilateral palpable, irregular, enlarged kidneys on abdominal exam; left costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis: 3+ blood, no significant proteinuria, no pyuria or nitrites. Bloods: Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (eGFR ~55), Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL (mildly reduced from baseline 13.5 g/dL). Renal ultrasound/CT shows innumerable bilateral cysts of varying sizes with a hyperdense, hemorrhagic cyst in the left kidney.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute hemorrhage into a renal cyst in a patient with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD).
reference_soap.plan: Conservative management: bed rest, oral hydration, and acetaminophen for pain (avoid NSAIDs). Continue antihypertensive therapy (Lisinopril) once hemodynamically stable; avoid anticoagulants during active bleeding. Monitor serial hemoglobin/hematocrit and vital signs; most hemorrhagic cysts resolve spontaneously within 2-7 days. If bleeding is refractory or hemodynamically significant, arrange renal angiography with selective embolization. Screen for intracranial aneurysm if family history of subarachnoid hemorrhage.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Polycystic Kidney Disease Cyst Hemorrhage
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for flank pain and visible blood in urine with family history of dialysis
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for nephrology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.diagnosis: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) with Cyst Hemorrhage
teaching.one_liner: A genetic disorder causing progressive growth of fluid-filled cysts in both kidneys; a cyst can suddenly bleed, causing acute flank pain and visible blood in the urine.
red_flags: Fever with flank pain — suggests infected cyst, a more urgent complication

must_ask.say: Does polycystic kidney disease or dialysis run in your family?
Where exactly is the flank pain, and did it start suddenly?
Is there visible blood in your urine?
Do you have a history of high blood pressure?

history.answer: My left side started hurting badly this morning, and when I went to the bathroom, my urine was red with blood.
It began suddenly early this morning, about six hours ago, and the dull, heavy ache has stayed steady since then.
I had a mild episode of reddish urine a couple of years ago that went away quickly, but this time the pain and color are much more noticeable.
It looks reddish-pink like cranberry juice throughout, without any visible dark clots.
The red color is present the entire time I pee, from the beginning to the end of the stream.
It doesn't hurt when the urine comes out, but I have a constant deep, heavy ache in my left flank.
The pain is located on my left flank just below my rib cage, and it does not shoot down to my groin or abdomen.
No burning, no urgency, and I'm not going to the bathroom any more frequently than usual.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweating.
No, my stream starts easily and feels strong, and I don't feel like any urine is left behind.
No, I haven't noticed any swelling in my face or legs, and my urine hasn't looked foamy or decreased in amount.
No, I haven't had a sore throat, runny nose, cough, or skin infections over the past several weeks.
No rash, no joint pain, and I haven't been coughing or coughing up blood.
No, my weight has been completely steady and I haven't felt unusually tired or run down.
No nosebleeds, no bleeding gums when I brush, and I don't bruise easily.
No, I do not take aspirin, warfarin, or any other blood thinners.
I haven't done any heavy workouts, haven't had any falls or back injuries, and haven't eaten beets or berries.
My last menstrual period finished about two weeks ago, so I am definitely not on my period right now.
I was diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease about eight years ago, but I have never had kidney stones.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure five years ago, and I take medication to keep it under control.
I thought I must be trying to pass a sharp kidney stone that tore something inside, given how suddenly the side pain hit and turned my urine red.
I watched my mother spend years tied to a dialysis machine, and I'm terrified that my kidneys are failing and that I won't be able to keep working.
Aside from polycystic kidney disease, high blood pressure, and slightly elevated cholesterol, I have no other health problems.
I had an appendectomy when I was in college, but I have never had any other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure, and no other medications or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine with dinner once or twice a month.
I work full-time in an office as an accountant and live with my husband and teenage daughter; no chemical exposures.
My mother and maternal uncle both have polycystic kidney disease, and my uncle is on dialysis.
My periods come regularly every twenty-eight days, my husband had a vasectomy, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg, pulse 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 37.0°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert and oriented, appearing uncomfortable due to left flank discomfort but in no acute respiratory distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are non-icteric without periorbital edema.
Abdomen is flat to slightly full in both flanks, symmetric, without distension or visible scars.
Bilateral large, irregular, nodular kidney masses are palpable, with mild tenderness over the left flank but no rebound tenderness or guarding.
Moderate left costovertebral angle tenderness is elicited on percussion; right costovertebral angle is non-tender.
No pretibial pitting edema or tenderness over either lower leg.
Warm, dry skin without rash, petechiae, purpura, or easy bruising.
